title: Visible-Centered Stack for Maximum Passband Transmission
scientific_hypothesis: A quarter-wave stack centered at 550 nm (visible band center) will achieve higher and flatter transmission in 420-700 nm than UV-centered designs, but UV and NIR stopband suppression will be weaker.
design_principle: Centering the Bragg condition at the passband center wavelength minimizes passband ripple by placing stopband edges symmetrically around the transmission window. This prioritizes signal collection over excitation suppression.
design_variables: individual layer thicknesses for all 36 layers, initialized near 550 nm quarter-wave condition (Ta2O5 ~96 nm, SiO2 ~147 nm), tuned during optimization
soft_objectives: keep individual layer thicknesses within 20-350 nm
manufacturing_considerations: thicker layers may reduce deposition time variation sensitivity
Ta2O5/SiO2 interface quality critical per L21
theory_basis: Bandpass filter design via symmetric stopband placement
expected_advantages: Highest visible passband transmission among the three routes
Flatter passband response for consistent fluorescence collection
Thicker layers may be more manufacturable
known_risks: UV stopband at 355-365 nm may be insufficient for excitation suppression
NIR stopband may fall outside effective reflection band
May require more layers to achieve equivalent stopband depth
execution_request_english: Design a 36-layer periodic dielectric filter on fused silica substrate with air incidence at 0 degrees, unpolarized light. Stack structure: Air | (Ta2O5 (Gao) | SiO2 (Gao)) repeated 18 times | Fused Silica. Initialize layer thicknesses near quarter-wave condition at 550 nm (Ta2O5 (Gao) approximately 96 nm, SiO2 (Gao) approximately 147 nm based on typical refractive indices). Optimize all 36 individual layer thicknesses within 20-350 nm bounds to maximize average transmittance in 420-700 nm while minimizing average transmittance in 355-365 nm and 1030-1080 nm bands. Report final layer thickness sequence and transmittance spectra across 350-1100 nm.
